segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jory Brennick, Liora Quill and Maud Brennick went over the side at first light, with two days left, and Walter Ames sat in the stern of Maud's boat holding the oars he had been told not to use. Jory carried the pry bar on a loop at his hip. Liora had an empty cask lashed across her back, bung driven home and waxed, which made her clumsy at the gap in the Kettle Row wall and did not improve her temper about it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Inside the back room the silt had settled overnight. The bench of cracked glass was where they had left it. The strongbox hung on the oak post at chest height, four bolts through its back plate into the wood.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jory got the bar under the head of the lowest bolt and leaned. Nothing. He shifted his grip and leaned again. The orange crust came away in a cloud, and the bolt turned a quarter and stopped. Above his head the ceiling boards were bowed down like a laden shelf, and that post was all that held them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Liora caught his wrist before the third pull and showed him the flat of her hand. Slowly. He nodded, and worked the bar in small bites after that, a finger's width at a time. Three bolts out, and the fourth took longer than the other three together. Maud hung back under the ceiling with both palms on the post, feeling for any give in it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The last bolt came free into Jory's glove. The box dropped two inches and he had it, and it went down through his arms like a wet sack of grain, and the post stood where it was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: An hour later they were back in the same room with the cask. Liora lashed it to the box, two turns and a hitch, and Maud hauled the knot tight with her heel braced on the floor. The cask took the weight and the box came up off the silt, swaying. The three of them walked it through the black water towards the green smear of the gap.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It would not go. Jory turned it on its corner, scraping stone. Then it went, and the pull of the cask took it up the wall faster than any of them could swim.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Liora broke the surface first and shouted, and Jory came up beside the hull with his hand already on the gunwale.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: It's up! Off your bow, Mr Ames, off your bow!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter Ames stepped over his own thwart and dropped to his knees at the bow. He got both arms over the side and his hands under the cask, and Maud came up on the other side to counter him. Between them the strongbox came over the gunwale and landed on the wet boards with a sound that was all stone and no wood.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It sat there dripping in the open morning. Harbour on all sides and nothing over it but sky.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: That's air. That's what she wanted. Nothing above it and nothing round it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walter knelt on the boards and put the oilcloth down beside his knee. He wiped the plate clear with his sleeve, twice, and took the breath a man takes before he says the first of three things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he stopped, and leaned closer, and brought the loupe up to his eye.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The letters were gone. Jory had put his hand flat on those letters two days ago and felt every one of them stand proud under his glove. The plate was smooth now, smooth as a river pebble, and dark, and the water ran off it without beading.
